prompt: A public good is
explanation: A public good is nonrival, so one person's use does not reduce another's use. It is also nonexcludable, so preventing nonpayers from benefiting is difficult.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: A common resource is
explanation: A common resource is difficult to exclude users from, but use depletes or crowds what remains for others. It is nonexcludable and rival.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: A club good is

options.label: D
options.text: Excludable and nonrival until congestion develops

options.label: E
options.text: Rival and excludable in every circumstance

explanation: A club good can exclude nonmembers. Over the relevant uncongested range, an additional user does not substantially reduce others' consumption, making it nonrival.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: Rivalry means that

options.label: A
options.text: One person’s use reduces availability to others

options.label: B
options.text: The good has a zero opportunity cost

options.label: C
options.text: Nonpayers can be prevented from receiving the good

options.label: E
options.text: The good creates an external benefit

explanation: Rival consumption reduces the amount or quality available to others. One person's use competes with another's.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: Excludability means that

options.label: A
options.text: One person’s use reduces the amount available to others

options.label: B
options.text: Government finances the good through taxes

options.label: C
options.text: The good is always socially efficient

options.label: D
options.text: Nonpayers can be excluded from the benefit

options.label: E
options.text: Every person receives the same benefit

explanation: Excludability means access can be restricted to paying or authorized users. It concerns who can use the good.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: The free-rider problem causes private firms to underprovide public goods because

options.label: A
options.text: Public goods are rival in consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Firms cannot charge for any private good

options.label: C
options.text: Benefits are accessible without revealing willingness to pay

options.label: D
options.text: Government provision eliminates all opportunity cost

options.label: E
options.text: Each additional user always raises marginal cost sharply

explanation: Nonpayers can benefit after others finance the good. This encourages free riding, leaving private revenue and provision below the good's social value.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: For a public good, society’s marginal benefit is found by

options.label: A
options.text: Subtracting marginal cost from each private benefit

options.label: C
options.text: Horizontally summing individuals’ quantities at each price

options.label: D
options.text: Using only the highest individual willingness to pay

options.label: E
options.text: Add individual marginal benefits at each quantity

explanation: Everyone benefits from the same supplied public-good quantity. Add each person's willingness to pay for that common quantity to calculate social marginal benefit.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: For a private good, market demand is found by

options.label: A
options.text: Add individual quantities demanded at each price

options.label: B
options.text: Vertically summing individual marginal benefits at each quantity

options.label: D
options.text: Using only the lowest willingness to pay

explanation: Private-good buyers can purchase different quantities. Add their quantities horizontally at each common price to obtain market demand.
reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: Government provision of a good does not necessarily make it a public good because

options.label: B
options.text: Rivalry and excludability determine the classification

options.label: D
options.text: Government provision makes marginal cost zero

reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: Free public schooling is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: A private service supplied free by government

options.label: B
options.text: A common resource because students remove the school

options.label: C
options.text: A club good with no possible congestion

options.label: D
options.text: A public good solely because taxes finance it

options.label: E
options.text: A pure public good because no student can be excluded

reference: POL-3.C | POL-3.C.1 | POL-3.C.2 | POL-3.C.3 | POL-3.C.4 | Skill 1.B

prompt: Based on the figure below, the efficient quantity of the public good occurs where

options.label: D
options.text: The two individual marginal-benefit curves intersect

options.label: E
